source: Druckman (2001) Using credible advice to overcome framing effects, JLEO 17(1):62-82
finding: Core claim: framing effects look large because lab subjects decide alone. Give them advice from a source they find credible and the effect shrinks or vanishes. Two experiments: Asian disease with party endorsements, and the McNeil lung-cancer problem with specialist endorsements.
numbers: Exp1 N=464 undergraduates, six conditions, party ID measured about 3 weeks earlier. Exp2 N=313 undergraduates, six conditions. Credibility of the sources was pretested.
quote: some widely known framing effects greatly diminish and sometimes disappear when participants are given access to credible advice
limits: Students only. Advice supplies information, so following it is not a violation of invariance (the author's own point). Only a minority of subjects follow the advice in full.
agent_relevance: A framed prompt plus a credible, checkable signal about which option is better is a different task from a bare framed prompt. Give the model evidence so the frame has less room to act.

source: Druckman (2001) JLEO, Experiment 1: Democrats (Asian disease with party labels)
finding: Democrats showed a big frame effect with neutral labels. A Democratic endorsement of the risk-averse program cut it by more than half. A Republican label on it cut it further.
numbers: Percent choosing the risk-averse option, gain vs loss frame. Neutral labels: 70% (N=30) vs 24% (N=34), reversal 46% (z=3.73). Democrats' program = risk-averse: 77% (N=39) vs 56% (N=34), reversal 21%. Republicans' program = risk-averse: 31% (N=39) vs 16% (N=37), reversal 15%.
limits: The effect did not fully vanish for Democrats (21% reversal, one-tailed p=.054). One-tailed tests. Cells are small (N 30-39).
agent_relevance: A source cue can swamp a wording frame. In a pipeline, cue strength may matter more than wording, so label provenance on purpose.

source: Druckman (2001) JLEO, Experiment 1: Republicans and Independents
finding: Republicans used the party cue and ignored the frame. Independents, who see neither party as credible, kept most of the framing effect.
numbers: Republicans, risk-averse choice: neutral gain 65% (N=20) vs loss 24% (N=21), reversal 41%. With Republican endorsement reversal 4%, with Democrat label 5%. Independents: neutral reversal 45% (z=2.94), with party labels 30% and 28%.
limits: Republican cells N=17-26; Independent cells N=14-26. The author notes Democrats seemed more frame-prone and gives only a partial explanation.
agent_relevance: Test of the moderator: no credible cue, no protection. If the model has no trusted signal, expect the frame to act in full.

source: Druckman (2001) JLEO, Experiment 2: McNeil lung-cancer problem with specialist advice
finding: Replicated the mortality vs survival frame effect with no advice. Credible specialist advice cut it to single digits whichever treatment was endorsed.
numbers: Percent preferring radiation. No advice: dying frame 44% (N=46) vs living frame 13% (N=53), reversal 31% (z=3.45). Surgery endorsed: 22% (N=50) vs 13% (N=55), reversal 9%. Radiation endorsed: 44% (N=50) vs 38% (N=55), reversal 6%.
limits: At least 56% always chose surgery and at least 13% always radiation, whatever the frame or advice. A few subjects got a non-credible source (insurance executive) and were not analysed in depth.
agent_relevance: Domain-expert cues are strong moderators. A cleaned prompt that states the expert consensus removes much of the frame effect.

source: Tversky & Kahneman (1981) Asian disease, as restated in Druckman (2001) JLEO
finding: Baseline founding numbers as restated by Druckman. The gain frame favours the sure program, the loss frame the gamble, though the programs are identical.
numbers: Gain frame: 72% chose program A (risk-averse), 28% program B (N=152). Loss frame: 22% chose program C, 78% program D (N=155). Shift about 50 points. McNeil et al. 1982: 44% chose radiation under the dying frame vs 18% under the living frame (26-point reversal).
limits: Quoted second-hand through Druckman. The 1981 Science paper and the 1982 NEJM paper were not opened.
agent_relevance: Reference size of the effect that any moderator must reduce.

source: Druckman (2001) On the limits of framing effects: who can frame? Journal of Politics 63(4), Experiment 1
finding: A humanitarian vs expenditures frame on aid to the poor moved opinion when attributed to Colin Powell, not when attributed to Jerry Springer. Source credibility is a precondition for an emphasis frame to work.
numbers: Overall opinion: Powell t(105)=2.21, p=.015; Springer t(101)=.55, p=.29. Importance of the poor's well-being: Powell 4.29 vs 5.13 (t39=1.75, p=.04); Springer 4.72 vs 4.91 (ns). Credibility pretested on 5-point knowledge and trust scales.
quote: perceived source credibility is a prerequisite for successful framing
limits: Emphasis framing, not equivalence framing. Student sample. One-tailed tests. Small cells.
agent_relevance: Frames from untrusted sources fail. In a multi-agent pipeline, weight inputs by source credibility.

source: Druckman (2001) JOP, Experiment 2: KKK rally tolerance, New York Times vs National Enquirer
finding: Same pattern on a second issue. Free-speech vs public-safety frames shifted tolerance when attributed to the New York Times, not to the National Enquirer.
numbers: NYT public safety vs free speech: tolerance difference t(34)=2.13, p=.02. Importance of opposing racism 2.56 vs 4.22; free speech 6.67 vs 5.61. National Enquirer: 3.35 vs 3.29 and 6.00 vs 6.06, no difference.
limits: Belief-content measures did not change in the credible conditions, so the frames worked by changing which considerations were weighted, not by persuasion. Control groups n=13-17.
agent_relevance: Frames act on what is weighted as important, not on facts believed. A cleaned prompt should restate the considerations neutrally.

source: Chong & Druckman (2007) Framing public opinion in competitive democracies, APSR 101(4)
finding: Frame strength, not repetition, drives the effect. Strong frames move opinion alone and win when two frames compete. Weak frames that invoke unavailable considerations do nothing.
numbers: Urban-growth experiment N=869; rally experiment N=1,277; 17 conditions; average n per condition in the rally experiment about 75. Availability pretest on 143 people: open space listed by 65%, economic costs by 73%, weak frames by 18% or less.
limits: Lab sample of students and community members. Opinion measures, not choices with stakes. A contrast effect (weak frame backfires) appeared only for knowledgeable respondents under a stronger opposing frame.
agent_relevance: Strength of the frame (availability and applicability), not volume, matters. Repeating a weak frame does not make it win.

source: Chong & Druckman (2007) APSR: knowledge and motivation as moderators
finding: Less-knowledgeable people were moved by weak frames in one-sided settings. Knowledgeable people dismissed them. Competition between frames made everyone evaluate more carefully.
numbers: Weak available frames moved low-knowledge respondents only in noncompetitive conditions (rally experiment). Low-knowledge respondents needed double exposure to the strong Pro frame before showing an effect (urban growth). Repeating a weak frame never let it beat a strong opposing frame. Two strong opposing frames pulled opinion to a midpoint proportional to their strength.
quote: Motivation and competition therefore offer complementary protections against arbitrary framing effects.
limits: Knowledge was measured, not manipulated.
agent_relevance: Showing the model both sides (a competitive context) is the analogue of listing counter-frames. Expect a smaller frame effect when both are present.

source: Chong & Druckman (2007) Framing theory, Annual Review of Political Science 10:103-126
finding: Theory: frames work through accessibility (priming a consideration) and applicability (judged fit). Motivated people weigh competing considerations. Competition motivates everyone. Credible sources raise the effect.
numbers: No new numbers. Cites Druckman 2001b for credible-source frames shifting opinion.
limits: Review of mostly emphasis-frame studies, not equivalence-frame choice tasks.
agent_relevance: Gives the two-route model: accessible content versus judged applicability. A scaffold step that asks whether a consideration applies targets the second route.

source: Kuhberger (2023) A systematic review of risky-choice framing effects, EXCLI J 22:1012-1031
finding: Size and robustness of the risky-choice framing effect. The 1998 meta-analysis found d=.31. A publication-bias corrected update found d=.52. Many Labs and a 100,000-person survey give about .60.
numbers: Kuhberger 1998: over 100 studies, over 200 effect sizes, about 30,000 participants, mean d=.31. Steiger & Kuhberger 2018: d=.52; 2016 studies d=.56. Many Labs (Klein 2014) d=.60. Im & Chen 2022: h=.612, 95% CI [.568, .656], over 100,000 people from 49 countries. In the 1981 original about 75% showed the effect and about 25% did not.
limits: Survey sample is not a lab. Attribute framing has no comparable meta-analysis (author says so). Many task variants.
agent_relevance: A real, medium effect that holds across samples. A quarter of people do not show it, so expect a mixture across model samples too.

source: Kuhberger (2023) EXCLI J: moderators and levels of equivalence
finding: Framing equivalence comes in levels (Sher & McKenzie). Even logically equivalent frames carry information when a speaker chooses them. Time pressure and System 1 reliance are said to raise the effect, deliberation to lower it, but thinking-style scales give no consistent pattern.
numbers: Time pressure raises the effect: Diederich et al. 2018, Roberts et al. 2022. Forced deliberation lowers it: Almashat et al. 2008. Thinking-style scales (REI, Need for Cognition, AOT, Faith in Intuition): 'no consistent picture'. Attribute framing diminishes or disappears when people get consumption experience (Poor & Isaac 2023).
limits: Review text. Individual studies not opened. The author argues the effect is adaptive, and notes that native vs foreign-language instruction is itself a (level 4) framing.
agent_relevance: A cleaned prompt must remove the speaker's choice of wording (level 2 information), not only surface words. Experience or data beats description.

source: Roberts, Teoh & Hutcherson (2022) Time to pay attention? Information search explains amplified framing effects under time pressure, Psych Sci 33
finding: Preregistered direct replication of Guo et al. 2017. A 1-second limit amplified the framing effect. Eye tracking says the cause is early attention to reward cues and truncated search, not an unchecked emotional system.
numbers: N=40 analysed (61 tested). Gamble choice with 1 s limit: gain .34 vs loss .64, d=1.52. No limit: gain .52 vs loss .64, d=.75. Frame x time interaction F(1,44)=57.06, p<.001. The change came entirely from more sure choices in gain trials (d=1.32); loss trials were unchanged (d=.003).
limits: Undergraduates, repeated-measures lab task with points. The reading challenges dual-system theory but does not refute it.
agent_relevance: The frame effect under a tight budget may come from reading less, not from a separate fast mode. A short context or short reasoning budget in an LLM may cut which attributes get read.

source: Gong, Wang, Ma & Lv (2026) How time pressure amplifies framing effects in risky decision-making, Behavioral Sciences 16(4):548
finding: Eye-tracking experiments with a 1-second limit. Time pressure amplified frame-consistent choices and cut fixation counts and durations. The introduction reports a mixed prior literature.
numbers: Exp1 N=26 analysed (30 recruited). Share of risky choices, gain frame: .11 under time pressure vs .36 without. Loss frame: .85 vs .49. Interaction F(1,25)=309.50, p<.001, partial eta-squared .93. Reaction time about 650-680 ms under pressure vs 2.0 s (gain) and 2.5 s (loss) without.
limits: Small sample; the effect sizes look very large. Chinese college students. The intro cites Svenson & Benson 1993 and Szaszi et al. 2022 among studies with limited or attenuated effects, and a four-decade meta-analysis (Belli et al. 2023) with heterogeneous effects moderated by task and frame.
agent_relevance: Time pressure is not a clean moderator. Direction depends on task and frame. Measure it for the model; do not assume.

source: Hinson et al. (2019) Working memory loads differentially influence frame-induced bias and normative choice in risky decision making, PLOS ONE
finding: A non-affective working-memory load produced large framing effects and worse accuracy. Affective loads, positive or negative, did not enlarge framing. The authors read framing as cognitive non-engagement more than affect.
numbers: 80 volunteers recruited, 76 analysed, aged 18-28. Load manipulation check F(2,54)=27.05, p<.0001; non-affective load accuracy .78 vs .99 and .98. Sure option of +5 or -5 against gambles of 33% or 67% for 20 or 80 points.
limits: Points-based gambles rather than words about lives. Single lab.
agent_relevance: Cognitive-load analogue: a crowded context may leave less capacity to check the problem. Keep the working prompt short.

source: Tennis players study (2025) Impact of framing effects, competitive state and time pressure on risk-taking decisions, Frontiers in Psychology
finding: Expertise moderates framing. Novices stayed frame-susceptible even under time pressure. Skilled players showed frame effects without pressure and turned conservative under pressure. Experts mostly followed the match situation.
numbers: Two experiments, each with 120 tennis players (40 expert, 40 skilled, 40 novice; 3:1 male to female).
limits: Only the abstract was read closely; no effect sizes extracted. Domain-specific task, not a standard wording frame.
agent_relevance: Domain knowledge replaces the frame with a model of the situation. A scaffold that supplies the domain state should displace the wording.

source: Diaz-Lago, Matute, Costa, Dunabeitia & Keysar (2018) Thinking in a foreign language reduces the causality bias (summary of Keysar 2012 and Costa 2014)
finding: Describes the founding foreign-language effect. People decide more systematically and with less loss aversion in a foreign language. Costa et al. 2014 replicated with the Asian disease problem and a money version (Financial crisis) and found less risk and ambiguity aversion and more consistent choices.
numbers: No new framing numbers. Their own data are on the illusion of causality.
limits: Secondary description of the framing studies.
agent_relevance: Weaker framing in a second language is the strongest sign that wording-driven bias can fall without new information.

source: Keysar, Hayakawa & An (2012) The foreign-language effect: thinking in a foreign tongue reduces decision biases, Psych Sci 23:661-668
finding: Founding paper. In an Asian-disease style problem, people reading it in a foreign language were less swayed by the gain or loss frame than people reading it in their native language. Authors proposed greater emotional distance and more deliberate processing.
numbers: Exact percentages and sample sizes not verified: the publisher page returned 403 and no open copy was found. About 476-514 citations (Semantic Scholar, Crossref).
limits: Not opened; described only through later papers.
agent_relevance: Wording effects shrink when the surface language is less fluent. A hint, not a recipe, for models: translation as debiasing is untested.

source: Costa, Foucart, Hayakawa, Aparici, Apesteguia, Heafner & Keysar (2014) Your morals depend on language, PLOS ONE 9(4):e94842
finding: Foreign-language use makes moral choices more utilitarian. The authors say the cause is a reduced emotional response and greater psychological distance. Same group as the framing foreign-language effect.
numbers: Abstract reports 'substantially more utilitarian decisions'. Per-experiment numbers were not extracted.
limits: Moral dilemmas, not framing. Included for the proposed mechanism.
agent_relevance: If the effect runs through emotion, text models may not benefit. Treat as untested.

source: Stibbard-Hawkes et al. (2024) Foreign-language effects in cross-cultural behavioral research: evidence from the Tanzanian Hadza, PNAS Nexus pgae218
finding: Foreign-language effects do not always keep their sign. With 129 Hadza participants given Hadzane or Kiswahili at random, the non-native language decreased risk preference on a wager and on Likert risk items, the opposite of earlier studies. Moral dilemmas gave the expected utilitarian shift.
numbers: N=129 Hadza participants, language assigned between participants. Moderate effect on wagers, substantial on dilemmas and risk Likert items.
limits: Not a framing task. Mechanism unclear (linguistic relativity or culture offered). One population.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: the direction of language effects depends on culture and task. Do not assume a fixed sign.

source: Deliberate reasoning is not affected by language (2019), PLOS ONE 14(1):e0211428
finding: Null result against the deliberation account of the foreign-language effect. On cognitive reflection, ratio bias, probability matching and base-rate items, second-language and switching groups did no better than native speakers.
numbers: Over 500 participants from Norway and the Netherlands (English as second language), randomised to native, switching or second-language conditions. All three performed equally well.
limits: No time pressure; the authors say an advantage may need it. Not a framing task.
agent_relevance: Competing explanation: if the effect is not extra deliberation it must run through emotion or fluency, which an LLM lacks in the same form.

source: Review (2023) Why should we study the foreign language effect: debiasing through affecting metacognition? J Intelligence 11(6):103
finding: Review of the foreign-language effect as debiasing. Foreign-language use reduced framing (Costa 2014; Winskel 2016) and made gambles more strategic (more bets when expected value is positive; Hayakawa 2019). The author says mechanism and limits are not understood.
numbers: No new numbers.
limits: Review by one author. The original studies were not opened. It notes that many debiasing techniques have limited effect or fix only one decision.
agent_relevance: Changing the input channel is a candidate debiasing step, but lasting benefit is unproven.

source: Suri, Slater et al. (2023) Do large language models show decision heuristics similar to humans? A case study using GPT-3.5, arXiv 2305.04400
finding: Study 3 tested a clinical gain vs loss frame on ChatGPT and 82 MTurk humans. Both showed a framing effect. ChatGPT was perfectly consistent across trials.
numbers: ChatGPT rated drug efficacy 5/7 in all 11 gain-frame trials and 4/7 in all 11 loss-frame trials. Humans: gain 5.2 (CI 5.03-5.37, n=44), loss 4.6 (CI 4.35-4.85, n=39), t(80)=3.86, p<.001.
limits: Attribute framing on a rating, not risky choice. 22 model trials with zero variance. ChatGPT would not give a direct decision so a rating was used. The authors suggest the effect may come from linguistic associations.
agent_relevance: Zero-variance output with a fixed one-point shift from wording alone. Look for a deterministic bias, not noise.

source: Binz & Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3, PNAS 120(6)
finding: GPT-3 was run on the Kahneman-Tversky problem pairs and scored by log-odds of choice probabilities. It showed 3 of 6 tested biases: framing, certainty and overweighting. It did not show reflection, isolation or magnitude-perception effects.
numbers: Six bias contrasts; positive log-odds on framing. Option order counterbalanced.
limits: GPT-3 from 2022; per-problem numbers not extracted. Hand-built vignettes.
agent_relevance: Base-model framing bias is the default. Newer instruction-tuned and reasoning models need their own test.

source: Echterhoff, Liu, Alessa, McAuley & He (2024) Cognitive bias in decision-making with LLMs, arXiv 2403.00811 (BiasBuster)
finding: In an admissions-officer prompt, GPT-4 admitted 40.5% more students when the same facts were framed as reject vs admit. Self-help debiasing (the model rewrites the prompt to remove bias) worked best.
numbers: Framing difference in admission rate for GPT-4: 40.5 points. After self-help, framing-biased prompts remained at 0% (Llama 2 13B), 1.4% (Llama 2 7B) and 2.7% (GPT-4). Awareness prompting cut GPT-3.5 framing and status-quo bias to 17.2% and 8.5%. Few-shot debiasing sometimes pushed models to admit or reject almost everyone (under 1% on one side).
limits: Synthetic admissions task. Models: GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama 2 7B and 13B. Self-help works best on higher-capacity models for some biases.
agent_relevance: Direct support for a cleaning step: have a model rewrite the problem neutrally, then decide on the rewrite. Few-shot examples can break the model.

source: Jones & Steinhardt (2022) Capturing failures of large language models via human cognitive biases, NeurIPS, arXiv 2202.12299
finding: Uses the framing effect as inspiration, not as a gain-loss test. Irrelevant preceding functions in a code prompt cut accuracy and the model copied the framing line.
numbers: Codex functional accuracy fell from 32.9% to 2.4-10.6% across five framing lines. The framing line appeared verbatim in 62.2-92.7% of Codex outputs and 58.2-79.3% of CodeGen outputs, against 0-11.5% unframed.
limits: Code generation, an analogy to framing rather than the Tversky paradigm. Models: Codex and CodeGen.
agent_relevance: Irrelevant leading context acts like a strong frame. Strip prompts of leading text before sampling.

source: Payne (2025) An analysis of AI decision under risk: prospect theory emerges in large language models, arXiv 2508.00902
finding: Five models (GPT-4o, o3, Claude Sonnet 4 with and without thinking, Gemini 1.5 Pro) showed framing effects that depend heavily on scenario. Reasoning models did not remove them. Effects were larger in military than civilian scenarios, and some civilian cases reversed.
numbers: 750 civilian and 1,000 military decisions, 25 iterations per cell. Championship-strategy framing effect +1.40 to +1.84 risk-score points across models; career transition -0.37 to -0.60 (reverse). Championship: loss frame 85.6% BLITZ vs gain frame 0.8%.
limits: Three-option scenarios, not the pure two-option paradigm. Gemini 2.5 Pro left out because it refused. Scenarios written by the author.
agent_relevance: Thinking mode does not guarantee frame robustness. Scenario meaning sets the sign and size.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) Same probabilities, different advice: gain-loss framing effects in high-stakes LLM decision support (FrameBench-HPS), arXiv 2610.29294
finding: 2,880 prompts from 240 scenarios (health, finance, education/career, legal). Gain vs loss phrasing of one probability changed the recommendation category in 32.4% of groups across seven LLMs. Almost all changes involved uncertainty, not a flip.
numbers: 32.41% category change (CI 30.48-34.36). Direct yes-no reversal 0.63%. 98.1% of 2,153 changes involved the 'uncertain' class. Per model: GPT-4o-mini 63.33%, GPT-5 33.40%, Gemini 2.5 Pro 32.56%, GPT-4.1-mini 29.17%, Gemini 3 Flash 23.38%, Claude Sonnet 4.6 22.81%, Qwen3-VL-235B 21.58%. Same-frame repeats disagree 7.12%; cross-frame 34.32%. Risk shift 0.535 at a 20% positive probability, 0.109 at 80%.
limits: Synthetic scenarios built with GPT-5 and checked. Temperature 0. Human check agrees on perceived risk shifts. Robustness runs used three models and 32 scenarios.
agent_relevance: The frame effect is about five times run-to-run noise. Framing matters most at low probabilities.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) FrameBench-HPS: probability canonicalization and frame-robust prompting, arXiv 2610.29294
finding: Showing both complementary probabilities in one standard form nearly removes the frame effect. Telling the model to compute the complement itself helps less.
numbers: Matched-repeat category change: original templates 36.81%, conversational 34.20%, canonicalization 6.68% (CI 5.12-8.51; paired drop 27.52 points), frame-robust prompting 22.83%. Mean risk shift .363 down to -.010 with canonicalization and to .154 with frame-robust prompting. Same-frame noise baseline 7.12%.
limits: Three models only (GPT-4o-mini, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Claude Sonnet 4.6), 32 held-out scenarios, three repeats. Only gain-loss probability framing, not emphasis or source framing.
agent_relevance: Cleanest answer so far to when a cleaned prompt is enough: when the frame is complementary-probability wording, a code step that writes both forms removes almost all of it. Put it in the scaffold as code, not model judgement.

source: Wang & Zhang (2026) Framing effects in independent-agent LLMs: a cross-family behavioral analysis, arXiv 2603.19282
finding: Two logically equivalent wordings of a threshold voting task (instrumental vs cooperative) gave opposite choices across 82 models in 11 families.
numbers: Option B chosen in 4.3% of trials under instrumental framing and 68.8% under cooperative framing. 20 independent trials per prompt per model.
limits: A game scenario where 'equivalent' is argued by the authors; wording also changes the social role. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Wording that sets the social role of the agent can dominate. Fix role text in code.

source: Lim, Kim & Whang (2026) DeFrame: debiasing large language models against framing effects, arXiv 2602.04306
finding: Fairness benchmarks augmented with alternate framings (for example 'A better than B' vs 'B worse than A') show scores vary with framing. Common debiasing prompts improve the average but not the frame gap. A framing-aware method cuts the gap.
numbers: 8 instruction-tuned models (Llama 3.x, Qwen2.5 3B to 14B, Gemma3, Mistral). DeFrame cuts framing disparity by 92% and bias score by 93% on average on BBQ.
limits: Fairness, not risk framing. Small open models only. Needs several calls.
agent_relevance: Average debiasing can hide a frame gap. Measure the difference between frames, not just the mean.

source: Germani & Spitale (2025) Source framing triggers systematic evaluation bias in large language models, arXiv 2505.13488
finding: LLM judges agree closely when blind, but agreement falls when told the author is Chinese or another LLM. Source attribution is a frame that models respond to, a loose analogue of Druckman's source credibility.
numbers: Four LLMs (o3-mini, Deepseek Reasoner, Grok 2, Mistral); 4,800 statements on 24 topics; 192,000 assessments. Attribution to Chinese individuals lowered agreement across all models, most for Deepseek Reasoner.
limits: Statement evaluation, not decisions under risk. Attribution framing, not equivalence framing. Preprint.
agent_relevance: LLM judges respond to claimed source. Hide authorship from any model judge, as G5 already requires.
